name: Addressing Router Interfaces
brief:
A router straight out of the box has no addresses and every interface administratively down. Two LANs are cabled to R1 and neither one can go anywhere until you address both interfaces and bring them up.

The PCs are already addressed. All the work is on the router.
watchFor: An address alone does nothing. Until you type `no shutdown` the interface stays administratively down, and `show ip interface brief` will tell you so in the Status column.

tasks.text: Address GigabitEthernet0/0 as 192.168.10.1 /24 and bring it up.
Address GigabitEthernet0/1 as 192.168.20.1 /24 and bring it up.
Run show ip interface brief and confirm both interfaces read up / up.
tasks.hint: Status and Protocol are two different columns. Both have to say up.

tasks.text: From PC1, ping PC2 at 192.168.20.20. Because both networks are directly connected to R1, no static routes are needed.
tasks.hint: A router always knows about the networks on its own interfaces. That is what the C code means in show ip route.

tasks.text: Save the configuration so a reload does not lose it.
tasks.hint: `copy running-config startup-config` from privileged EXEC, then press Enter at the filename prompt.

extension: Shut GigabitEthernet0/1 and run show ip route. Explain why the 192.168.20.0/24 route disappears from the table even though the address is still configured.
debrief: Two directly connected networks route between each other for free, because a router puts every up interface network into its routing table automatically. The moment an interface goes down, that route leaves the table. This is the fastest way to understand what a C route actually means.
